title: Chest Pain

rationale.Physical Exam: General Appearance: Gauge how sick the patient may be.
rationale.Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs: Investigate for lung pathology. Pleuritic pain may have pulmonary origin.
rationale.Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular: Cardiac pathology often causes chest pain — must examine. Listen for pericardial friction rub.
rationale.Physical Exam: Abdomen: Pain radiating to back — abdominal exam needed.
rationale.Physical Exam: Extremities / Spine: Look for edema or pathology guiding workup.
rationale.Physical Exam: HEENT / Neck: GERD or esophageal pathology could cause symptoms.
rationale.Pulse oximetry: Check oxygenation if concerned about circulation.
rationale.ECG, 12 lead: ECG on every chest pain patient. Will show diffuse ST elevation in pericarditis (not territorial like MI).
rationale.Cardiac troponin I, serum: Must rule out MI in chest pain. Negative in pericarditis.
rationale.Echocardiography (transthoracic): TTE shows small pericardial effusion. Transthoracic is sufficient — TEE is unnecessary and invasive.
rationale.Chest X-ray: Rule out other causes of chest pain.
rationale.ANA, serum: Autoimmune etiology is one cause of pericarditis.
rationale.Echocardiography, transesophageal: TTE is more than sufficient. TEE is invasive and unnecessary for small pericardial effusion — points lost for ordering.
rationale.NSAIDs (Ibuprofen / Naproxen / Aspirin): NSAIDs are treatment of choice for acute pericarditis.
rationale.Colchicine: Added to NSAID therapy — reduces symptoms AND decreases rate of recurrent pericarditis. Well tolerated. Should be added for first-episode acute pericarditis.
rationale.PPI / H2 blocker (Omeprazole / Famotidin: High-dose NSAID therapy requires GI protection with PPI or H2 blocker.
rationale.Pericardiocentesis: Only small effusion — will resolve on its own. Pericardiocentesis only for moderate/large effusions (>2 cm) or tamponade.
rationale.Advise patient, rest at home: Activity may trigger recurrence. Rest until symptoms resolve.
rationale.Transesophageal echocardiography: Invasive and unnecessary. TTE is sufficient to evaluate pericardial effusion. Ordering TEE loses points.
rationale.NSAIDs alone (without colchicine): Colchicine should be added to NSAID therapy for first-episode acute pericarditis — it reduces recurrence rate and improves symptom resolution.
rationale.Glucocorticoids as first-line: Steroids are reserved for refractory pericarditis unresponsive to NSAIDs/colchicine, or autoimmune-associated pericarditis.

hpi: {{patient_name}} is a man with no significant past medical history who presents with acute chest pain that is pleuritic (worse with inspiration) and positional (relieved by leaning forward). He has no history of recent viral infection, making this likely idiopathic pericarditis. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation. Echocardiogram reveals a small pericardial effusion — no tamponade physiology. Troponin is negative, ruling out MI. First-line treatment: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) PLUS colchicine — colchicine reduces symptoms and decreases rate of recurrent pericarditis. Add a PPI/H2 blocker for GI protection with high-dose NSAID therapy. Rest until symptoms resolve — activity can trigger recurrence. Pericardiocentesis is NOT indicated for small, asymptomatic effusions (only for moderate/large effusions > 2 cm or tamponade). Transesophageal echo is unnecessary — transthoracic echo is sufficient.

case_summary: Idiopathic acute pericarditis. Pleuritic chest pain + diffuse ST elevation + small effusion on echo. NSAIDs + colchicine + PPI. Avoid pericardiocentesis and TEE. ER then outpatient management with rest.
